pageTitle: When clocks disagree, whose time is it?

paper.title: On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies

summary: Einstein starts with a puzzle about magnets and moving wires, then asks how distant clocks can agree. His principles lead to a new way to compare space and time in steadily moving frames.

hook.teaser: Why can a magnet and a wire seem to tell two stories about the same electric current?

blocks.deck: Einstein starts with a magnet-and-wire puzzle, then asks how distant clocks can share a time.

blocks.title: A new way to compare motion

chapters.title: A magnet, a wire, and a mismatch
chapters.caption: Move a magnet near a wire and a current appears. Describe the wire as moving while the magnet rests, and the current can be the same—but the usual explanation changes. Einstein wants the laws of moving bodies described without giving one viewpoint special status. Grown-up words: electromotive force; electrodynamics.

media.alt: Magnet-moving and wire-moving setups appear side by side with matching current arrows and the question “Same current. Why different?”

chapters.title: Set distant clocks with light
chapters.caption: A nearby clock gives a local time. For distant clocks, Einstein defines a synchronization rule: send light from A to B, reflect it back, and set the clocks so both parts of the trip take equal time. Grown-up words: synchronization; simultaneity.

media.alt: Two distant clocks and a light signal traveling from A to B and reflecting back.

chapters.title: Two principles
chapters.caption: The laws of nature work the same in steadily moving frames. Light in empty space has the same speed in a frame whether its source is still or moving. These are the two principles Einstein uses to build the account in this paper. Grown-up words: principle of relativity; constancy of the velocity of light.

media.alt: Two steadily moving frames with a light ray, illustrating the principles named in the paper introduction.

chapters.title: Clocks and rods compare differently
chapters.caption: The paper derives what its principles mean for moving clocks and rods: for the clock setup analyzed in section 4, the other frame’s observer finds a small slowing, approximated there when higher-order terms are neglected. The paper also derives a shorter measured length for a rod along its direction of motion. These are theoretical consequences, not measurements reported in this paper. Grown-up words: time dilation; length contraction.

media.alt: A moving clock and a rod aligned with motion, compared from another frame.

facts.text: Einstein compares a magnet moving near a conductor with a conductor moving near a magnet; the current can be the same although the usual explanations differ.
The clock-synchronization definition uses a light signal sent to a second clock and reflected back, with equal outward and return travel times.
The paper starts from the relativity principle and the constancy of light speed.
For the clock-transport setup in §4, Einstein derives a small difference between the carried clock and the one left at B; his calculation uses a small-speed approximation.
The paper derives that a rod’s measured length along its motion is shorter in the other frame.
